naturalness.evidence: “What were the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath commanded to do?” is idiomatic English. Both “going off duty” and “commanded to do” are familiar expressions and require no mental repair.

processing.evidence: Readers must hold “What were” across the subject “the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath” until reaching “commanded to do.” They must also identify the divisions as both receiving the command and performing the requested action. These are ordinary, manageable operations; the modifier identifies the relevant divisions rather than adding avoidable load.

context_economy.evidence: The question contains no extra introductory framing. “Going off duty on the Sabbath” usefully identifies which two divisions are being asked about.

structure_assessments.reason: In “the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath,” the adjacent modifier naturally describes the divisions, and “on the Sabbath” naturally specifies when they go off duty. This is useful identification with no competing attachment that requires repair.

“Were ... commanded to do” is a familiar passive construction. Understanding the divisions as command recipients and as performers of the commanded action requires ordinary role tracking, not substantial avoidable effort.
